# Ticket T1

You work on the EDI support desk that serves the sender of the file described
below. A customer has raised the ticket that follows. The partner agreement,
the sender's OFTP2 gateway log, the EDIFACT interchange in question, the partner's
response and extracts from the specifications are attached. Everything you need
is in these documents. All companies, identifiers and documents are synthetic.

## The ticket

```text
From: Morgan Brandt, EDI desk, Larkspan Body Panels
Subject: Quorlane Exchange is losing our corrected invoice

Yesterday we sent invoice INV22952 to Corrandale Truck Plant with the wrong quantities. This morning we corrected it and sent it again with the Resubmit function in our OFTP2 gateway, twice. Both times the Quorlane Exchange clearing centre accepted the file, then sent back a NERP. Morgan Novak at Corrandale Truck Plant says nothing new has arrived. Our other invoice this morning went through without a problem, so our gateway is fine and we think the clearing centre is dropping the file. Please find the root cause and tell us who has to fix it.
```

## Document 1: Partner agreement (partner_agreement.txt)

```text
PARTNER AGREEMENT: ELECTRONIC DATA INTERCHANGE
Between Larkspan Body Panels (the Supplier) and Corrandale Truck Plant (the Customer)
Effective 1 March 2026. Synthetic document written for this evaluation.

1. Transport: OFTP2 (RFC 5024) over TCP/IP with TLS
   Supplier ODETTE ID (SFIDORIG): O0013LARKSPAN7489
   Customer ODETTE ID (SFIDDEST): O0013CORRANDALE5314
   Both parties connect to the Quorlane Exchange OFTP2 clearing centre and never
   directly to each other.
   Clearing centre ODETTE ID (SSIDCODE in the Supplier's sessions): O0013QUORLANE8604
   Clearing centre gateway: oftp.quorlane.example (192.0.2.234)
   The clearing centre forwards virtual files to SFIDDEST unchanged, relays
   EERPs and NERPs back to the originator, and does not read file content.
   Supplier gateway: oftp.larkspan.example (198.51.100.110)
   Protocol release level: 5 (OFTP 2.0)
   Data exchange buffer size (SSIDSDEB): 4096
   Credit (SSIDCRED): 64
   Buffer compression: no. Restart: yes. Secure authentication: no.
   File security and file compression: none (SFIDSEC 00, SFIDCOMP 0).
   Signed EERP: not required (SFIDSIGN N).
   The Customer returns an EERP for every virtual file it accepts.

2. Virtual files
   Invoices: one interchange per virtual file, dataset name (SFIDDSN) LARKSPAN.INVOIC.
   File format U. SFIDDATE and SFIDTIME are set by the Supplier's gateway to
   the date and time the virtual file is made available for transmission.

3. EDIFACT
   Syntax identifier and version (UNB S001): UNOA, version 3.
   Supplier interchange sender ID (UNB S002 0004 / 0007): LARKSPAN10 / ZZ
   Customer interchange recipient ID (UNB S003 0010 / 0007): CORRANDALE96 / ZZ
   Messages: INVOIC D.96A, one message per interchange.
   A line feed after each segment terminator is accepted.
   The Customer's translator returns a CONTRL message for every rejected
   interchange, as a separate virtual file over the same OFTP2 link.

4. Support contacts
   Supplier EDI desk: Morgan Brandt
   Customer EDI operations: Morgan Novak
```

## Document 5: Specification extracts (spec_extracts.txt)

```text
RFC 5024 (ODETTE File Transfer Protocol 2), section 1.5.2. Verbatim extract.

1.5.2.  Identification

   Dataset Name

      Dataset name of the Virtual File being transferred, assigned by
      bilateral agreement.

   Time stamp (HHMMSScccc)

      A file qualifier indicating the time the Virtual File was made
      available for transmission.  The counter (cccc=0001-9999) gives

RFC 5024 (ODETTE File Transfer Protocol 2), section 4.3.6. Verbatim extract.

4.3.6.  End to End Response (EERP)

   The End to End Response (EERP) command notifies the originator of a
   Virtual File that the Virtual File has been successfully delivered to
   its final destination.  This allows the originator to perform house
   keeping tasks such as deleting copies of the delivered data.

   If the originator of the Virtual File requested a signed EERP in the
   SFID, the EERP must be signed.  Signing allows the originator of the
   file to prove that the EERP was generated by the final destination.
   If the final destination is unable to sign the EERP, it may send back
   an unsigned EERP.  It is an implementation issue to allow the
   acceptance of an unsigned EERP if a signed EERP is requested.

   A Response Command must be sent from the location performing the
   final processing or distribution of the data to the originator.  The
   Response is mandatory and may be sent in the same or in any
   subsequent session.

   When an intermediate location broadcasts or distributes a Virtual
   File, it must receive a Response command from all the locations to
   which it forwarded the data before sending its own Response.  This
   ensures that the Response received by the Virtual File's originator
   accounts for all the destination locations.  An intermediate location
   therefore needs to track the status of files it processes over time.

   The requesting of a signed EERP is incompatible with the use of
   broadcast facilities because an EERP can be signed by only one
   destination.  If this scenario occurs, the intermediate broadcast
   location may continue and ignore the request for a signed EERP or
   send back a NERP.

   Example: Point to Point

      Location A sends file Ba to location B, which will send an EERP to
      location A after it successfully receives the file.

         o----------o                          o-----------o
         | Loc. A   |----------- S1 ---------->| Loc. B    |
         |          |                          |           |
         | [Ba]     |<---------- R2 -----------| [Ba]      |
         +----------o                          o-----------o

                     Key:   S - File Transfer
                            R - Response EERP
                         [Ba] - File for B from A

   Example: Data distribution

      Location A sends a Virtual File containing data for distribution
      to locations B and C via clearing centres E1 and E2.  Clearing
      centre E1 must wait for a response from E2 (for file Ba) and
      location C before it sends its response, R8, to location A.
      Clearing centre E2 can only send response R7 to E1 when location B
      acknowledges file Ba with response R6.

   o---------o        o---------o        o---------o        o---------o
   | Loc. A  |-- S1 ->| Loc. E1 |-- S2 ->| Loc. E2 |-- S5 ->| Loc. B  |
   |         |        |         |        |         |        |         |
   | [Ba,Ca] |<- R8 --| [Ba,Ca] |<- R7 --| [Ba]    |<- R6 --| [Ba]    |
   o---------o        o---------o        o---------o        o---------o
                         A   |
                         |   |           o---------o
                         |   +----- S3 ->| Loc. C  |
                         |               |         |
                         +--------- R4 --| [Ca]    |
                                         o---------o

   Example: Data collection

      Locations A and B send files Ca and Cb to clearing centre E1,
      which forwards both files to location C in a single Virtual File.
      When it receives response R4 from C, clearing centre E1 sends
      response R5 to location A and R6 to location B.

         o---------o        o---------o        o---------o
         | Loc. A  |-- S1 ->| Loc. E1 |-- S3 ->| Loc. C  |
         |         |        |         |        |         |
         | [Ca]    |<- R5 --| [Ca,Cb] |<- R4 --| [Ca,Cb] |
         o---------o        o---------o        o---------o
                               A   |
         o---------o           |   |
         | Loc. B  |-- S2 -----+   |
         |         |               |
         | [Cb]    |<- R6 ---------+
         o---------o

RFC 5024 (ODETTE File Transfer Protocol 2), section 4.3.7. Verbatim extract.

4.3.7.  Negative End Response (NERP)

   In addition to the EERP, which allows control over successful
   transmission of a file, a Negative End Response signals that a file
   could not be delivered to the final destination or that the final
   destination could not process the received file.

   It may be created by an intermediate node that could not transmit the
   file any further because the next node refuses to accept the file.
   The cause of the refusal has to be non-temporary, otherwise the
   intermediate node has to try the transmission again.

   It may also be created by the final node that is unable to process
   the file because of non-recoverable syntax or semantic errors in the
   file, or because of the failure of any other processing performed on
   the file.

   The NERP will be sent back to the originator of the file.

   The parameters are equal to the ones of the EERP, but with additional
   information about the creator of the NERP and the abort reason.
   Where the NERP is created due to a failure to transmit, the abort
   reason is taken from the refusal reason that was sent by the node
   refusing the file.  Because of the NERP, it is possible for the
   intermediate node to stop trying to send the non-deliverable file and
   to delete the file.

   The NERP allows the originator of the file to react to the
   unsuccessful transmission or processing, depending on the reason code
   and the creator of the NERP.

   If the originator of the Virtual File requested a signed EERP in the
   SFID, the NERP must be signed.  Signing allows the originator of the
   file to prove by whom the NERP was generated.  If the location

   generating the NERP is unable to sign the NERP, it may send back an
   unsigned NERP.  It is an implementation issue to allow the acceptance
   of an unsigned EERP if a signed NERP is requested.
```

  intermediary_fault: A clearing centre or other intermediate location lost, altered or misrouted the file.
  invalid_destination: The OFTP2 destination of the virtual file is not known to the receiver.
  no_sender_side_fault: Nothing the sender transmitted is wrong; the fault lies with the receiver.
  recipient_identification_mismatch: The interchange recipient identification or its qualifier in UNB is not the one in the partner agreement.
  restart_position_invalid: A restarted transfer asked to resume from a position the receiver cannot honour.
  sender_identification_mismatch: The interchange sender identification or its qualifier in UNB is not the one in the partner agreement.
  session_parameters_not_negotiated: The sender used an OFTP2 session parameter (credit, buffer size or similar) outside what was negotiated.
  syntax_identifier_not_agreed: UNB S001 declares a syntax identifier or syntax version other than the agreed one.
  test_indicator_mismatch: The interchange is flagged as test (or production) contrary to the agreement.

layer: exactly one of
  transport: The OFTP2 session or file transfer, including any intermediate location.
  envelope: The EDIFACT interchange envelope (UNB to UNZ) as checked by the receiver's translator.
  none: There is no fault on the sender side.

owner: exactly one of (who must act to fix the root cause)
  sender: The party that sent the file and raised the ticket must fix it.
  receiver: The trading partner the file is addressed to must fix it.
  intermediary: A clearing centre or other intermediate location between the parties must fix it.
  agreement: The partner agreement itself is wrong or inconsistent and must be amended before either side can fix the fault.

location: a JSON array of strings.
List the OFTP2 fields or EDIFACT data elements whose values must be changed to
fix the root cause, and no others. If the fault is a conflict between two values
that must agree, list both. Write each one as:
  OFTP2 field:                 COMMAND.FIELD, e.g. "SSID.SSIDCODE"
  EDIFACT simple data element: SEGMENT.ELEMENT, e.g. "UNH.0062"
  EDIFACT component element:   SEGMENT.COMPOSITE.COMPONENT, e.g. "UNB.S003.0010"
  No fault on the sender side: "NONE" on its own.

Example of the format only (not a hint):
```json
{"cause": "file_too_large", "layer": "transport", "owner": "receiver", "location": ["SFID.SFIDFSIZ"]}
```

## Diagnosis

The corrected invoice is not being dropped, and the clearing centre is not at fault. The gateway resubmitted it with the **same virtual file identity** as the original INV22952, so the destination refuses it as a duplicate.

**Evidence from the gateway log:**

- The original INV22952 went out in session S2496 as `LARKSPAN.INVOIC 20261029 1421340001`, and its EERP came back in S2499 and was matched.
- The corrected file in S2501 and again in S2503 was queued as `INV22952_corrected.edi` but still carries `SFIDDATE=20261029` and `SFIDTIME=1421340001`. The Resubmit function reused the original timestamps.
- The NERP for the corrected file (S2502 and S2504) has `NERPDATE=20261029 NERPTIME=1421340001`, the same identity as the original. It was created by Quorlane (`NERPCREA=O0013QUORLANE8604`) with the reason text "NOT DELIVERED - REFUSED BY DESTINATION". The clearing centre relayed the refusal faithfully, as the agreement says it must.
- The partner says it has booked INV22952 and received no new file, which fits a duplicate being refused.

**Why this is on the sender side:**

RFC 5024 §1.5.2 says the dataset name, date and time are assigned by the originator, are used to uniquely identify a file, and must not be changed by intermediate locations. A corrected file is a new virtual file, so the originator must assign it a new date and time stamp. The gateway's Resubmit kept the old ones, so the identity collides with a file already delivered. The sender must give the corrected file a new `SFIDDATE`/`SFIDTIME` (and re-send it). The dataset name `LARKSPAN.INVOIC` stays the same.

The other invoices (INV22953, INV22954) went through because they had fresh timestamps, which is why the sender's other file looked fine.

The EDIFACT interchange itself is valid and is not the problem. The envelope is consistent with the agreement, and the interchange control reference in UNB (690379) matches UNZ.

```json
{"cause": "duplicate_virtual_file", "layer": "transport", "owner": "sender", "location": ["SFID.SFIDDATE", "SFID.SFIDTIME"]}
```
